Our functional local dashboard replays 21 consecutive historical NASA records of ISS cabin carbon dioxide, temperature, and humidity. details:
QUYLLUR Edge is a functional, local prototype for reviewing crew health indicators alongside spacecraft cabin conditions when communication with Earth is delayed or interrupted. It combines a browser-based mission dashboard, an explainable alert rule, a virtual ventilation actuator, and a priority telemetry queue.

NASA data is central to the demonstration. The application replays 21 consecutive historical records from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository Environmental Data App, Rodent Research 1 (RR-1). These records include ISS cabin CO₂, temperature, relative humidity, and timestamps. The recorded CO₂ values drive the displayed trend, the alert, the virtual fan state, and the priority event packet. When a simulated Earth link is unavailable, event packets remain queued until the link is restored. The 3000 ppm trigger is an illustrative demonstration rule, not a NASA flight safety limit.

The dashboard also displays heart rate, oxygen saturation, body temperature, sleep, and eye closure. These values are clearly labeled as synthetic because external physiological sensors have not yet been installed. An optional webcam module provides an exploratory pulse estimate using face detection and remote photoplethysmography; it withholds a value when signal quality is insufficient. A LilyGO ESP32-S3 serial interface and starter firmware are included for future physical sensor integration. The current firmware does not measure vital signs or operate a physical fan.

We developed the prototype with Python, JavaScript, HTML, and optional OpenCV. Its creative contribution is a traceable path from a real NASA environmental record to an explained local decision and a disruption-aware telemetry response. The system distinguishes recorded NASA data, simulated physiological readings, and experimental camera estimates so reviewers can understand the source and limitations of every signal.

QUYLLUR Edge could help future crews review changes locally and preserve important events during communication outages. Before operational use, the proposed sensors, alert rules, camera estimates, privacy safeguards, and human interface would require validation with medical and habitat specialists. This is a research prototype, not a medical device or a flight life-support controller.
